title: Fluoroquinolone + antacid chelation: decreased drug bioavailability (treatment failure)
vignette: A 64-year-old man comes to the office for follow-up after a recent hospitalization. Ten days ago, he was admitted due to fever, dysuria, urinary urgency, and perineal pain. Evaluation revealed acute prostatitis, and urine culture was positive for Escherichia coli that was sensitive to all tested antibiotics. He received intravenous ciprofloxacin with improvement in his symptoms and was subsequently discharged on oral ciprofloxacin. The patient has been taking the antibiotic as prescribed, but over the past 2 days he has had recurrent fever and dysuria. He takes diltiazem for palpitations, atorvastatin for hyperlipidemia, and an over-the-counter antacid for frequent heartburn. Temperature is 37.3 C (99.1 F), blood pressure is 118/68 mm Hg, and pulse is 90/min. Physical examination shows a mildly enlarged and tender prostate. Repeat urine culture grows E coli. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's recurrent symptoms?

clues.note: Fluoroquinolones are highly bioavailable orally but their absorption is markedly reduced by chelation with polyvalent cations.
Antacids contain polyvalent cations (calcium, magnesium, aluminum) that form insoluble chelates with fluoroquinolones in the gut, blocking absorption.

clues.text: Repeat urine culture grows E coli
clues.note: The SAME organism recurs; the initial isolate was pan-sensitive and IV therapy worked - pointing to failed drug delivery (absorption), not resistance.

whatMatters: Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin) form INSOLUBLE CHELATES with polyvalent cations (Ca, Mg, Al) found in ANTACIDS, drastically reducing oral absorption. The patient responded to IV cipro but relapsed on oral cipro taken with an antacid - failure from DECREASED BIOAVAILABILITY, not resistance. Answer B.
strategy: The IV drug worked and the organism stays pan-sensitive, so the drug is effective when it reaches the blood - the problem is ORAL ABSORPTION. Fluoroquinolones (and tetracyclines, levothyroxine) chelate antacid cations -> decreased bioavailability. Reject acquired resistance (culture still sensitive; relapse coincided with the oral switch), sexual reinfection (E coli prostatitis, older man - not typical), increased renal clearance (switching IV->oral doesn't change clearance), and CYP induction (cipro is renally eliminated; not the mechanism).

eliminations.label: Acquired resistance - culture still sensitive
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the organism developing fluoroquinolone resistance. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: the isolate remained pan-sensitive and he initially responded; relapse coincided with the switch to oral therapy taken with an antacid, indicating an absorption problem rather than resistance. ✅ Correct if: repeat culture shows new fluoroquinolone resistance.

eliminations.label: Untreated sexual partner - not the mechanism
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: reinfection via sexual transmission. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: E coli prostatitis in an older man is not sexually transmitted (that pattern fits gonorrhea/chlamydia in younger men); this is treatment failure of the same infection. ✅ Correct if: STI prostatitis in a younger man.

eliminations.label: Increased renal clearance - switch doesn't change clearance
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: faster renal elimination lowering drug levels. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: changing from IV to oral does not increase renal clearance; the drop in effect is due to reduced ORAL absorption. ✅ Correct if: a clinical change that truly raised clearance (rare).

eliminations.label: CYP induction - cipro is renally cleared
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: enzyme induction lowering drug levels; diltiazem is actually a CYP3A4 INHIBITOR, not inducer. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: ciprofloxacin is eliminated mainly by the kidney and is not significantly affected by CYP induction; the interaction here is gut chelation. ✅ Correct if: a CYP-metabolized drug losing effect from an inducer (rifampin).

reasoning: IV ciprofloxacin worked and the E coli stayed pan-sensitive
Relapse began after switching to ORAL ciprofloxacin taken with an antacid
Fluoroquinolones chelate antacid cations (Ca/Mg/Al) -> insoluble complex -> poor absorption
-> decreased oral bioavailability caused treatment failure; answer B
mechanism: FLUOROQUINOLONES (e.g., ciprofloxacin) normally have high oral bioavailability, but they form INSOLUBLE CHELATE COMPLEXES with POLYVALENT CATIONS - CALCIUM, MAGNESIUM, ALUMINUM, IRON - in the gastrointestinal tract. Over-the-counter ANTACIDS (and calcium supplements, iron, sucralfate, dairy) contain these cations, so co-administration markedly DECREASES fluoroquinolone ABSORPTION and BIOAVAILABILITY, leading to subtherapeutic levels and treatment failure. This patient responded to INTRAVENOUS ciprofloxacin (which bypasses the gut) but relapsed after switching to ORAL ciprofloxacin taken with an antacid, while the E coli remained pan-sensitive - a classic drug-drug interaction rather than acquired resistance. The same chelation interaction affects TETRACYCLINES and LEVOTHYROXINE. Management is to separate the antibiotic from cation-containing products by several hours. The distractors (resistance, sexual reinfection, increased renal clearance, CYP induction) don't fit: the culture stayed sensitive, ciprofloxacin is renally eliminated, and diltiazem is a CYP inhibitor, not an inducer.

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Pharm > fluoroquinolones: chelate with Ca/Mg/Al/Fe (antacids, dairy, supplements) -> decreased absorption; separate dosing; same interaction with tetracyclines/levothyroxine.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Cipro + antacid cations -> insoluble chelate -> poor absorption -> treatment failure (not resistance).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on bioavailability, chelation, polyvalent cations, fluoroquinolone, or drug-drug interaction? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Culture still sensitive (not resistance); IV->oral doesn't change clearance; cipro is renally cleared (not CYP); not an STI.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: fluoroquinolones/tetracyclines/levothyroxine chelate antacid cations -> decreased bioavailability; separate doses.

keywords.front: IV worked but oral failed, same sensitive bug

keywords.back: Separate antibiotic and cation product by several hours

firstAid.detail: Pharm: antacid cations reduce absorption -> decreased bioavailability.
Pharm/Micro > resistance vs absorption vs clearance vs CYP.

memoryHook: Cipro and antacids clump into a useless brick in the gut - the drug never gets absorbed, so the infection roars back even though the bug was never resistant.
